clinicalPearls: A rare, fulminant variant of the antiphospholipid syndrome in which widespread small-vessel thrombosis produces multi-organ failure evolving over a very short period, typically days.

Classification requires involvement of multiple organs or systems developing near-simultaneously, histopathological confirmation of small-vessel occlusion, and the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies confirmed on testing.
An identifiable precipitant is common and includes infection, surgery or trauma, withdrawal or inadequacy of anticoagulation, malignancy, pregnancy and the puerperium, and lupus flares.
The clinical picture frequently overlaps with thrombotic microangiopathy, with thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic haemolysis and red-cell fragments on the blood film.
Renal involvement is very common, but cerebral, pulmonary, cardiac, cutaneous, gastrointestinal and adrenal disease all occur, and adrenal haemorrhage can cause acute insufficiency.
First-line management combines anticoagulation with heparin, high-dose corticosteroids, and plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, alongside vigorous treatment of any precipitating trigger.
Refractory or lupus-associated disease may respond to rituximab or complement blockade with eculizumab.
It is distinguished from classical antiphospholipid syndrome, which tends to cause discrete large-vessel thrombosis rather than a diffuse small-vessel thrombotic storm.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder arises when antiphospholipid antibodies, principally lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies, drive a self-amplifying thrombotic storm affecting predominantly the microvasculature. A widely invoked two-hit model holds that the circulating antibodies provide a persistent prothrombotic first hit by activating endothelial cells, platelets and monocytes and by upregulating tissue factor, while a second hit such as infection, surgery or anticoagulation withdrawal ignites explosive intravascular coagulation. Activation of the complement cascade is central, generating anaphylatoxins that further injure endothelium, recruit neutrophils and amplify thrombin generation, and the resulting cytokine surge produces a systemic inflammatory response that compounds tissue ischaemia. Diffuse small-vessel occlusion across many organs simultaneously leads to the characteristic picture of rapidly progressive multi-organ failure, and the thrombotic microangiopathic features reflect mechanical red-cell fragmentation and consumptive thrombocytopenia within the occluded microcirculation. This mechanistic emphasis on complement and endothelial activation underlies the rationale for combining anticoagulation and immunomodulation, and for complement inhibition in resistant disease.
additionalDifferentials: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and haemolytic uraemic syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Lupus anticoagulant assays with anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies in immunoglobulin G and M classes
Full blood count and blood film for thrombocytopenia and red-cell fragments
Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and D-dimer
Renal and liver function with urinalysis
ADAMTS13 activity to help exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Biopsy of an affected organ demonstrating small-vessel thrombosis without vasculitis
Antinuclear and anti-double-stranded-DNA antibodies and complement levels to assess for associated lupus
redFlags: Rapidly progressive failure of several organs over days
Respiratory failure or the acute respiratory distress syndrome
Encephalopathy, seizures or focal neurological deficit
Acute kidney injury with malignant hypertension
Features of adrenal insufficiency or adrenal haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Mortality is high even with treatment, but early institution of combined anticoagulation, corticosteroids and plasma exchange or immunoglobulin substantially improves survival. Survivors remain at risk of recurrent thrombosis and require sustained anticoagulation.
pitfalls: Attributing the picture solely to sepsis or disseminated intravascular coagulation and missing the underlying antiphospholipid syndrome
Withdrawing anticoagulation, which is itself a recognised trigger of the catastrophic event
Delaying triple therapy while awaiting confirmatory antibody results
Overlooking adrenal involvement as a cause of unexplained deterioration
Failing to identify and treat a precipitating infection or other trigger
references: Standard rheumatology and haematology reference texts
International consensus guidance on catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome
